DAMASCUS: Syria reopened its main border crossing with Jordan on Wednesday (Oct 28) as the two countries reaffirmed ties that were strained by a deadly retaliatory strike by Jordanian forces. Jordan's strike - a reprisal against a gun attack on a church - sparked the worst crisis between the two countries since the ousting of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. Syria condemned the strikes on the country's south as an "unacceptable violation", while Jordan said it killed more than 20 militant fighters in its raid. Jordan sought to ease tensions on Tuesday, saying it had "great respect" for its neighbour and expressed regret for civilian casualties.

The main Nassib border crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, was closed following the strikes, but passenger and commercial movement will return to normal as of Wednesday morning, senior Syrian customs official Mazen Alloush told state news agency SANA. Last week, gunmen opened fire during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan's Karak governorate, killing nine people and wounding 25 - prompting a military response from Amman. While Jordan insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus denied the claim, and Syria's civil defence agency said the raids killed seven people, including three children. On Tuesday, Jordan's Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi spoke to his Syrian counterpart and emphasised Jordan's "full respect for Syria's sovereignty ... and security", while also expressing "sorrow and grief over the death of innocent civilian victims", according to a joint statement. The two officials also discussed the raids against what the statement branded as "Daesh sites", using an acronym to refer to the Islamic State (IS) group. Earlier, Jordan's government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani had said that "the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh's ranks - estimated at more than 20 fighters". He also said "a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation" had been destroyed. "BLATANT VIOLATION" Earlier, Syria's foreign ministry issued a "condemnation and rejection" of the strikes, calling them "an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination". It also said the raid was "a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty". In the coming days, a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet to discuss the operations against IS, a government source told Syrian state news agency SANA. Syria said five people, including a woman and three children, were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south. "We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children - two boys and a girl - were killed," said Nassouh al-Salim in Al-Taf, staring at a grey body bag. An AFP reporter saw a huge crater in the family's destroyed home, with school books, clothes and the remains of furniture strewn among the rubble. Syrian Emergencies and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Tuesday that both sides were handling the dispute through "diplomatic and legal channels" with the aim of securing justice for the victims. "DARK IDEOLOGIES" On Monday, Amman said authorities had arrested three Jordanians accused of the church killings , two of them brothers and the other related by marriage. Authorities said the suspects were hospitalised after being wounded in a shootout with security forces. Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three per cent of the population. "We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," King Abdullah II said. IS was territorially defeated in Syria in 2019, after it seized swathes of territory during the country's more than 13-year civil war. But remnants are still present, and the group occasionally claims attacks, mainly targeting Syrian security forces. The group has previously been present in parts of Daraa province.

Source: Reuters/ec

VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo will meet with survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy during his Nov 6 to 17 three-country tour of South America , the Vatican said on Tuesday (Oct 27). The pontiff , who is recovering from lung cancer surgery , will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on one of the most intense foreign trips taken by a pope in decades, after being deemed fit for the journey by his doctor on Monday. "Several meet ings are planned with people who have been victims of abuse by members of the clergy and the Church," the Vatican said in its Tuesday statement. "These meet ings reflect the pope 's desire to express his closeness to those who have suffered, and who still suffer, because of this violence," it said. Pope Leo , 71, has held meet ings with survivors of abuse by clergy on several of his foreign visits, including in France last month. In that encounter, the pope met for two hours with seven French victims and reaffirmed his commitment to ending abuse of children by Catholic priests, the Vatican said afterwards. Pope Leo , originally from the US, served as a missionary and bishop in Peru for decades before becoming the head of the Catholic Church .

LONDON: GSK said on Tuesday (Oct 27) that it expects to almost double the number of cancer medicines it has in clinical trials next year , including those in early-stage studies, as it tries to rebuild its oncology business. The drugmaker's clinical -stage portfolio of about 15 assets would likely "come close to doubling" in 2027, Hesham Abdullah, who heads GSK 's oncology research and development, told the Wall Street Journal earlier on Tuesday. The British drugmaker has bet big on cancer drugs under CEO Luke Miels, including its US$10.6 billion takeover of US biotech Nuvalent earlier this year . One of the drugs acquired in the process received approval in July while a regulatory decision on another is expected by November. Miels faces the task of reassuring investors that the company can navigate looming patent cliffs for its blockbuster HIV drugs.

"We may have close to 20 phase threes ongoing in 2027," Eric Richards, who heads oncology product development at GSK , told Reuters earlier in the week at a medical meeting. Cancer drugs such as ris-rez and mo-rez are at the centre of GSK 's ambitions. On Monday, data from GSK and Hansoh's ris-rez showed that it helped patients with a hard-to-treat cancer live longer without the disease worsening. Five late-stage studies for mo-rez are ongoing as are two of four planned late-stage trials for ris-rez. Cancer drugs contributed £1.08 billion (US$1.44 billion) to GSK 's first-half sales. The company is due to report third-quarter earnings on Wednesday.

HEBRON, West Bank: Israeli troops fired a stun grenade on Tuesday (Oct 27) to disperse Palestinians who gathered to protest against an Israeli military operation that has displaced thousands of residents from a neighbourhood in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. The unrest, which follows the deaths of two Israeli soldiers shot by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint last week, unfolded as Israelis were voting in an election in which the country's posture in the West Bank has been a major political issue. Some Palestinian officials have accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of launching a crackdown in the West Bank to coincide with the vote, as a way to energise his right-wing supporters. The government says its operation is a response to the attack on its soldiers. A group of Palestinian men, women and children gathered at Tuesday's protest. One elderly man held a placard that said: "No to collective punishment, no to closures, and no to displacement."

The military said it had fired a stun grenade to disperse them so that its operation could continue.

A Palestinian man holds a placard which reads: "No to collective punishment / No to closure and no to displacement" during a protest in Hebron in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Oct 27, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Mussa Qawasma)

On Monday, the United Nations said that over 3,000 Palestinians had been forced from their homes by the Israeli military operation, which targeted neighborhoods near the checkpoint where Palestinian gunmen killed the two Israeli soldiers on Friday. "Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," said UN human rights chief Volker Türk in a statement. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing." The Israeli military said in a statement on Sunday that troops would carry out demolitions in the area. It said soldiers had not located any weapons in searches of the houses. Since Friday's attack on the checkpoint, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns across the West Bank, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement. Noura Nassar, a displaced resident who attended the protests, said she had struggled to get medical treatment because of the blockages. "Where is the democracy in all of this? Their elections are today, sure, but what about us? Aren't we human beings? We want to go out, we want to visit the doctor," said Nassar.

A child looks at a banner depicting Israeli Prime Minister and Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu, during the country's national elections in Jerusalem, Oct 27, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Ronen Zvulun)

Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot both oppose the creation of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. Residents expelled from the Hebron neighbourhood said Tuesday's election in Israel would do little to change the reality on the ground in territories Israel has occupied since 1967. "Among themselves they will elect who is the oppressor and who will destroy the Palestinian people. That is their election," said Sana' Salman Abu Sneineh, another expelled resident. Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements, which are deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Under Netanyahu's right-wing coalition there has also been a surge of militant settler violence against Palestinians.

BEIJING: China is highly concerned about conflicts in the Middle East and surrounding regions and Beijing will send an envoy to the relevant countries in the near future, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a daily press conference on Tuesday (Oct 27). Guo called on related parties to resolve differences through dialogue and negotiation and also expressed concerns about the spillover and transmitting of the Middle East conflict to the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region. "China will soon send a special envoy to visit countries in the regions to strengthen communication with relevant parties, promote contact and dialogue, help ease tensions and prevent the situation from deteriorating further," Guo said. Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the Gulf kingdom. Meanwhile, tensions between the US and Iran have sharpened recently with President Donald Trump saying last week that his country may strike Iran again. Last week, the foreign ministers of China and Djibouti met in Beijing, where they agreed that easing tensions in the Middle East is key to addressing security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea.

Source: Reuters/ec

The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo has risen above 10,000, government data showed on Tuesday (Oct 27), a milestone that coincides with growing fears the epidemic could spread to more African countries. The latest situation report from Congo's public health institute put the number of cases at 10,060, with those killed by the virus reaching 4,887. The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, was announced in mid-May and has since become the largest and deadliest in Congo, surpassing a 2018-2020 epidemic. It is now the second-largest and second-deadliest on record behind only the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000, mainly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Earlier this month, Kenya reported its first case and went on to announce nine cases in total, after a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda died in Nairobi. Last week, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case. Health officials have been seeking to work out how and where the patient - the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who had not travelled to Congo - contracted the disease. The Swiss government said she was believed to have contracted it in Uganda. The woman and her husband were flown to hospitals in Switzerland on Monday. Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August. Ugandan officials say the country does not have any Ebola cases. Uganda's health minister said on Sunday that Ugandan citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to Congo would be quarantined for 21 days.
